stories.title: Great Lakes and Ontario: waterways, villages and treaty country
stories.subtitle: Fish fences, longhouse villages, canoe commerce and colonial institutions reveal a Great Lakes world built through work, diplomacy, conflict and continuing Indigenous community life.
stories.description: Fish fences, longhouse villages, canoe commerce and colonial institutions reveal a Great Lakes world built through work, diplomacy, conflict and continuing Indigenous community life.

scenes.title: A small stone with a distant source
scenes.body: Two obsidian flakes from a submerged Lake Huron setting connect this region to a geological source in Oregon. They are small objects with a large historical implication: materials could travel across networks extending thousands of kilometres. The evidence identifies the stone’s source, not a single traveller or an exact exchange route. Around the early-Holocene lake, shorelines differed from today’s, and places now underwater once formed part of a lived landscape of movement, work and knowledge.
scenes.note: Viewing year within the existing dated context; no direct transcontinental route is drawn.

scenes.title: Building with water and fish
scenes.body: Wooden stakes at Mnjikaning preserve the work of fish-fence builders at the Narrows between Lakes Simcoe and Couchiching. The earliest dated evidence is placed around 3300 BCE. Concentrated seasonal fish runs made the channel a place where practical skill and collective responsibility mattered. Later Wendat use and Anishinaabeg stewardship belong to its history as well. The marker points to the surrounding public locality, while the surviving underwater structures retain their own protected locations and significance.
scenes.note: Approximate early-use anchor; not a continuous 5,000-year occupation interval.

scenes.title: Objects, food and ceremony around Rice Lake
scenes.body: The Serpent Mounds complex preserves more than the outlines of earthworks. Pottery, pipes, stone points, worked bone and antler, and food refuse connect ceremony with the everyday activities of people living around Rice Lake. The selected Point Peninsula phase falls between about 50 BCE and 300 CE. These material remains reveal skilled making and a place repeatedly invested with meaning. They do not turn an archaeological label into one timeless people or pinpoint individual graves on this map.
scenes.note: Year 100 is a viewing point within the published phase.

scenes.title: A village’s date changes the history
scenes.body: At Jean-Baptiste Lainé/Mantle, longhouses enclosed a central plaza and defensive works protected the settlement. A new radiocarbon model places the site later than its former circa 1500–1550 dating. This changes how we understand the timing of community aggregation near Lake Ontario. The village contained few European goods, but that absence did not mean it was early or isolated. Different communities participated in different networks, and the histories of their exchange relationships cannot be read from a single imported object.
scenes.note: 1596–1618 is a 68.2% modeled date estimate, not an occupation-duration estimate.

scenes.title: Attack, displacement and survival
scenes.body: In March 1649, attacks on Saint-Ignace and Saint-Louis devastated Wendat villages. Saint-Louis was a lived settlement, with longhouses, hearths, stored food, defences and a mission presence. The Jesuit headquarters at Sainte-Marie was burned and abandoned later that year. Those destroyed buildings mark a crisis, but they do not mark the end of Wendat people. Communities reorganized in different places; the history leading to Wendake belongs alongside the events in Huronia, with survivors and their descendants remaining central.
scenes.note: The mission and village are distinct places; no single dispersal route is inferred.

scenes.title: Water routes link work and war
scenes.body: By 1812, the lakes linked several kinds of political and economic activity. Haudenosaunee communities had been established along the Grand River after the American Revolution, and Haudenosaunee allies took part in the defence at Queenston Heights. Farther west, Fort William gathered Indigenous suppliers, voyageurs and North West Company partners for the fur trade. Canoe routes, portages and provisions joined these worlds, while the people involved pursued interests that cannot be reduced to a simple French-versus-British map.
scenes.note: The scene connects regional contexts; displayed lines should remain schematic or absent.

scenes.title: Treaty relationships and a school
scenes.body: At Sault Ste. Marie, the Robinson-Huron Treaty negotiations of 1850 addressed land, payments, reserves and livelihoods under growing pressure from mining and settlement. In 1875, the rebuilt Shingwauk Home opened nearby. The two records concern different institutions, but both show how colonial authority entered Indigenous life. Shingwaukonse’s educational aspirations should remain distinct from the residential school’s assimilation project. The school’s later history and the work led by Survivors help explain what happened to children behind an administrative opening date.
scenes.note: The school opening is documented. The map ends in 1900 and supplies no closure date.

scenes.title: Signing away access on paper
scenes.body: At Rama on 7 November 1923, commissioners and community representatives signed one stage of the Williams Treaties. The written terms addressed claims to land and harvesting rights across a large area already affected by settlement and extraction. Set beside Mnjikaning’s fish fences, the treaty makes a deep change visible: the ability to obtain food and maintain relationships with water and land became subject to colonial restrictions. A signing place is a point on the map; the consequences reached far beyond it.
scenes.note: Historical treaty text is not presented as a resolution of modern legal rights.

stories.title: Québec and the St. Lawrence: villages, alliances and living homelands
stories.subtitle: Follow stone-working places, farming villages, river diplomacy and colonial land changes while keeping the histories of Indigenous communities visible beyond every change of regime.
stories.description: Follow stone-working places, farming villages, river diplomacy and colonial land changes while keeping the histories of Indigenous communities visible beyond every change of regime.

scenes.title: Tools along an older river world
scenes.body: Rimouski and Kruger 2 preserve stone points, fragments, bifaces and other tools from early communities in Québec. Their settings belong to landscapes changing after the ice retreated. Finished pieces show skilled shaping; unfinished ones bring us closer to the work of manufacture. These finds are evidence of people using particular places, not a complete map of ancient nations or languages. They give the St. Lawrence story a long beginning before written descriptions of villages and colonial arrivals become available.
scenes.note: The existing records use broad regional chronology; 9000 BCE is only a viewing year.

scenes.title: Households and craft at McDonald
scenes.body: McDonald’s longhouses and middens preserve the material traces of a St. Lawrence Iroquoian village. Bone tools and the waste left while making them reveal an economy of skill: food animals also supplied materials for needles, awls and other implements. The published phase is approximately 1335–1380 CE. Villages in this region combined cultivation with fishing, hunting and gathering. A later move to another place need not mean a people vanished; changing settlement locations can be part of an ongoing community history.
scenes.note: A municipality-scale reference protects the exact archaeological locality.

scenes.title: A larger longhouse village
scenes.body: Droulers/Tsiionhiakwatha preserves a larger settlement than nearby McDonald. A primary artifact study describes seven excavated longhouses and two middens, with abundant worked bone and animal remains. More houses may have existed, but the excavated number is the secure observation. The study’s circa 1490–1515 phase differs from the visitor centre’s circa 1450 date. The architecture and artifacts remain compelling across that disagreement: many households lived, cooked, made tools and negotiated their relationships within a substantial village.
scenes.note: Uses the newer study’s approximate phase; the older public chronology remains documented.

scenes.title: Visitors meet supplied villages
scenes.body: Cartier’s account describes fish, beans, bread, gifts and an open gathering space at Hochelaga. At Stadacona, houses held winter supplies, and communication depended partly on Taignoagny and Dom Agaya, who had already endured being taken to France. These were encounters with organized communities, not discoveries of vacant riverbanks. Nearby archaeological sequences, including Mailhot-Curran, provide a material history alongside the written account. The chronicles contain useful details, but their visitors’ perspective cannot stand in for everyone who lived through the encounter.
scenes.note: Distinct villages and sources are compared, without identifying an archaeological site as Hochelaga by assumption.

scenes.title: Anadabijou receives the French
scenes.body: At Pointe aux Alouettes in 1603, Anadabijou’s gathering brought Innu participants together with Anishinabeg and Etchemin allies. Champlain and Gravé du Pont entered this established diplomatic world. The agreement gave French activity a place within Indigenous alliances; it did not make Tadoussac a place without a previous history. Trade and transshipment developed around waterways already used for meetings and travel. The marker uses Tadoussac for orientation, while the documented gathering was across the Saguenay mouth at Pointe aux Alouettes.
scenes.note: The public locality anchor is deliberately distinct from an exact meeting spot.

scenes.title: Community rebuilding and regional diplomacy
scenes.body: Wendake’s establishment in 1697 belongs to the history of Huron-Wendat survival and new community life after upheaval in the Great Lakes. Four years later, Wendat diplomacy helped shape the Great Peace of Montréal. Kondiaronk and other Indigenous leaders did political work across long distances, alongside French authorities and delegates from many nations. These events show the river as a connection between living communities. They also show that an agreement grew from negotiation among participants whose interests and experiences were not identical.
scenes.note: The city marker represents the agreement, not a reconstructed conference footprint.

scenes.title: A war enters homes
scenes.body: The 1759 war cannot be told only through the battlefield outside Québec. At Odanak, Rogers’s Rangers attacked a fortified Abenaki community, burning buildings and killing inhabitants. Community remembrance includes the women, children and elders harmed there. The Plains of Abraham and the later battle of Sainte-Foy changed the military balance, but those outcomes were also experienced in homes and communities. Odanak’s rebuilding, including a new wooden church in 1760, prevents the story from ending with the flames of the raid.
scenes.note: No disputed casualty total or exact battle geometry is asserted.

scenes.title: Boundaries laid over older homelands
scenes.body: The Kitigan Zibi allotment step of 1853 and the Pointe-Bleue exchange of 1856 show how colonial land administration defined reserves inside older homelands. At Mashteuiatsh, Pekuakamiulnuatsh history records a choice shaped by pressure on earlier reserved lands and attachment to the lakeshore. At Kitigan Zibi, the official acreage tells us what a distribution list proposed, not the whole extent of Anishinabe life. By the twentieth century these communities continued, while reserves and government institutions constrained their relationship to land and livelihood.
scenes.note: Administrative dates do not date the origin of either people or homeland.

stories.title: Atlantic Canada: coastal communities, fisheries and displacement
stories.subtitle: Follow coastal tools, Indigenous sea hunting, Atlantic fisheries, Acadian displacement and a mission established among Inuit in 1771.
stories.description: Follow coastal tools, Indigenous sea hunting, Atlantic fisheries, Acadian displacement and a mission established among Inuit in 1771.

scenes.title: Stone tools after the ice
scenes.body: Debert’s stone tools belong to an early history of people using Atlantic landscapes after the ice retreated. A calibrated synthesis puts its pooled age around 12,630 years before 1950. The site is often pictured as a caribou-hunting place, but its excavations did not recover animal bones. The tools provide direct evidence; the hunted species requires interpretation. This distinction leaves the human story intact while keeping it honest: people worked here, shaped stone and knew a landscape very different from Nova Scotia today.
scenes.note: Approximate viewing year within the existing calibrated range, not a newly calculated first arrival.

scenes.title: Sea hunting and sacred places
scenes.body: At Phillip’s Garden, house remains, middens and seal bones show Dorset communities making a living beside the sea. Bone measurements support hunting in more than one season. Farther southwest, Metepenagiag’s Augustine Mound preserves ceremonial objects and knowledge carried between generations. These are distinct communities, periods and forms of evidence, joined here by a coastline and river world that held many ways of living. Neither an archaeological label nor a single mound should replace the history of people who continue to care for place.
scenes.note: Augustine Mound remains an undated context record because its source dates cannot be rendered as a closed interval; year 100 concerns the Phillip’s Garden viewing position.

scenes.title: A precise year of woodworking
scenes.body: Three pieces of wood from Norse archaeological contexts at L’Anse aux Meadows preserve an unusually precise date. Researchers identified a radiocarbon event in annual tree rings and counted outward to the cutting edges: the trees were cut in 1021 CE. This anchors a real episode of work at the settlement. It does not tell us when every building was erected, how long every crew remained, or when all contact began. The precision belongs to the documented activity, not to every part of the site’s story.
scenes.note: Reuse the existing precise-date record; do not duplicate the alternative Norse visit pin.

scenes.title: Turning whales into an Atlantic commodity
scenes.body: At Red Bay, Basque crews hunted whales during seasonal expeditions and processed them ashore. Rendering ovens, cooperages, wharves and temporary quarters formed a system for producing oil and loading barrels for Europe. Wrecks preserve another part of that work beneath the water. The station’s sixteenth-century remains allow us to connect ships with labour on land, rather than treating maritime history as voyages alone. The surrounding Labrador coast also held Indigenous histories that were neither begun nor completed by these seasonal industrial visits.
scenes.note: 1560 is a viewing year within a rounded sixteenth-century activity phase.

scenes.title: Several communities share an Atlantic age
scenes.body: Port-Royal’s French habitation and Ferryland’s English plantation belonged to different colonial projects, each embedded in a maritime economy. Their foundation dates do not tell the whole regional story. At Boyd’s Cove, Beothuk housepits show an Indigenous community living on Newfoundland during the seventeenth and early eighteenth centuries. Across these places, houses, fisheries, trade and seasonal movement made different patterns. The map keeps each chronology separate so that the growth of colonial settlements does not make Beothuk or Mi’kmaq communities disappear from view.
scenes.note: The scene compares historical contexts; it does not make the 1605 and 1621 establishments occur in 1680.

scenes.title: Conquest becomes forced departure
scenes.body: The capture of Fort Beauséjour in 1755 and the confinement of Acadians at Grand-Pré connected military power with civilian removal. Three years later, after Louisbourg fell, British authorities organized deportation from Skmaqn/Port-la-Joye on Île Saint-Jean. Families left an island that had also been a place of Mi’kmaq–French alliance. More than 3,000 French and Acadian inhabitants were removed, and shipwrecks and illness killed many at sea. The departures changed communities across the Atlantic while Mi’kmaq life on Epekwitk continued under new pressures.
scenes.note: These are related events in 1755 and 1758, not a single voyage or one deportation day.

scenes.title: A mission arrives where Inuit live
scenes.body: Nunatsiavut’s history states clearly that Inuit were living at Nain when Moravian missionaries arrived in 1771. The mission became a centre for trade and religious activity, adding institutions that influenced the community’s later buildings, music and spiritual life. Its establishment therefore belongs inside Inuit history, not in place of it. Nain also offers a different kind of colonial encounter from the forts and deportations farther south. Distinct experiences along the Atlantic coast should remain visible even when they share a chronological map.
scenes.note: The date marks the mission; it does not mark the origin of the Inuit community.

scenes.title: Children taken into an assimilation system
scenes.body: Shubenacadie residential school opened to students in 1930, after construction in 1928–1929. Many Mi’kmaw and Wolastoqkew children were compelled to attend the federally funded, church-run institution. Its purpose reached beyond instruction: it was part of a system seeking to suppress Indigenous cultures and identities. The official history was developed with representatives acting for Survivors and descendants. The atlas ends in 1934, but the school remained open much longer, and the histories of affected families and communities cannot be confined to that map endpoint.
scenes.note: Opening-to-students event; never display 1934 as the school’s closing date.

stories.title: Pacific Canada: shorelines, villages and colonial encounters
stories.subtitle: Footprints, clam gardens, houses, trade and Indigenous communities across the coast and Fraser interior.
stories.description: Footprints, clam gardens, houses, trade and Indigenous communities across the coast and Fraser interior.

scenes.title: Footsteps on a changing shore
scenes.body: A child-sized footprint and larger impressions turn an early coastline into a place where people can be imagined moving, pausing and stepping across wet ground. The Calvert Island assemblage contains 29 identifiable tracks, with associated pine wood dating the surface. It is a brief physical trace within a much larger human history. Changing shorelines help explain why early coastal evidence can be buried or difficult to find, while the tracks themselves do not supply a complete route or settlement history.
scenes.note: Viewing year lies inside the conservative dated envelope; island reference only.

scenes.title: Building a more productive beach
scenes.body: At northern Quadra Island, low stone walls changed how sediment accumulated along the shore. The resulting terraces enlarged suitable clam habitat and required knowledgeable work with local tides and beach conditions. The dated gardens reveal deliberate food production in Laich-Kwil-Tach and northern Coast Salish homelands. Their history stretches through many construction and maintenance episodes. Reading a wall alongside the shells beneath it and former sea levels is how researchers distinguish an old beach from a garden made and tended by people.
scenes.note: Rounded conservative minimum-age anchor, not the first wall’s exact year.

scenes.title: Life inside large housepit villages
scenes.body: Keatley Creek brings the journey inland to substantial houses near the Fraser. Excavations distinguish house floors, deposits and rebuilding histories, giving archaeologists material for studying households and social differences. The timing of the large village remains debated: one model includes significant breaks, while another interpretation argues for a longer development. At this viewing date the focus is the evidence for village life and its complexity. The remains should not be read as every visible house occupied simultaneously by one precisely counted population.
scenes.note: 800 CE is a viewing year within the named model, not a construction date.

scenes.title: Diplomacy at a Mowachaht centre
scenes.body: Ships reaching Yuquot entered an existing Mowachaht political and ceremonial centre. The late eighteenth-century sea-otter trade attracted merchants, while British and Spanish competition brought negotiations between Vancouver and Quadra in 1792. These events make sense together: trade, diplomacy and local authority occupied the same harbour. The established Yuquot records connect this meeting with a broader decade of maritime exchange. The scene does not turn a European visit into the founding of the community or make visiting powers the only actors in its history.
scenes.note: The map follows this date across every region; zoom out to see other histories.

scenes.title: Cedar houses and a commercial fort
scenes.body: Nineteenth-century wooden buildings served very different purposes across the coast. At SG̱ang Gwaay, Haida houses and carved poles expressed household and community relationships. On the lower Fraser, Fort Langley moved from fur trade toward supplies, fish packing and farming, then hosted the proclamation of the mainland colony in 1858. Looking across these places reveals existing Indigenous centres alongside expanding colonial institutions. Their shared use of timber does not imply a common political system, and the surviving remains belong to different building histories.
scenes.note: 1858 is the scene’s contextual date; Langley’s record dates its 1827 establishment.

scenes.title: War chiefs executed at Quesnel
scenes.body: Five Tŝilhqot’in war chiefs were hanged at Quesnel in October 1864 after entering colonial custody during an invitation to discuss peace. Their nation’s history places the conflict within defence of land and people. Later provincial acknowledgments recognize the wrongful treatment. This is a specific act of colonial violence, with named political actors and a documented place and date. It should remain distinct from Ahan’s execution the following year and from the many other ways Tŝilhqot’in people sustained their communities through colonial change.
scenes.note: The map follows this date across every region; zoom out to see other histories.

scenes.title: Ceremony under the potlatch ban
scenes.body: Dan Cranmer’s 1921 potlatch at ʼMimkwa̱mlis brought people together while Canadian law criminalized their ceremony. Prosecution and confiscation followed, removing masks and other belongings whose significance included histories, family responsibilities and public performance. Nearby Alert Bay also held St. Michael’s residential school, documented from 1894. These institutions and interventions affected different parts of community life. U’mista’s account keeps the ceremonial gathering and its participants central, showing that repression encountered people actively maintaining practices rather than a culture that had already disappeared.
scenes.note: The gathering is 1921; confiscation followed in 1922.

stories.title: Prairie Canada: foodways, Métis settlements and treaty encounters
stories.subtitle: Hunting, cultivation, river-lot communities, treaties and colonial institutions across the northern plains.
stories.description: Hunting, cultivation, river-lot communities, treaties and colonial institutions across the northern plains.

scenes.title: Horses and camels at a river crossing
scenes.body: At Wally’s Beach, hunters processed horses and a camel beside an ancient crossing. Cut marks, broken bones and artifacts allow researchers to reconstruct practical work with large animals. Revised radiocarbon analysis places that activity around 13,300 calibrated years before 1950. This scene is about the evidence left by butchering, rather than a complete reconstruction of the hunt. The animals’ later extinction raises larger questions that one locality cannot answer by itself, and several nearby carcasses need not all represent the same day.
scenes.note: Rounded calibrated-age anchor.

scenes.title: What hunters carried back
scenes.body: Near the Souris River, the Atkinson site preserves a processing place with a hearth, tools and bison remains. The interpretation emphasizes selected portions carried into camp, making transport and preparation visible alongside hunting. The published calibrated chronology lies in the fifth millennium BCE. A camp can record skilled choices about food and work without being the place where animals died. Read with Alberta’s Quarry of the Ancestors, this evidence also helps connect the making and use of tools with food procurement across different landscapes.
scenes.note: The quarry record is comparative earlier evidence, not synchronous with this camp.

scenes.title: Maize, hoes and stored harvests
scenes.body: At Lockport, maize kernels, bison-bone hoes and storage pits show cultivation beside Red River fishing grounds. These are complementary activities at a strategically useful place. Later evidence south of Melita extends the farming story into southwestern Manitoba, where the Olson site yielded additional hoes. Neither locality needs to be forced into a single cultural label. Together they reveal northern agricultural knowledge and the labour of planting, tending and keeping food, while leaving detailed community connections open to further investigation and discussion.
scenes.note: 1400 is within Lockport’s phase; Olson is a later comparison, not yet dated to 1400.

scenes.title: Pemmican and political rights
scenes.body: The encounter at Frog Plain took place within a trade economy sustained by Indigenous food, transport and labour. Cuthbert Grant’s Métis party was moving provisions when it confronted Governor Semple’s party in June 1816. Métis accounts remember the resulting victory as a declaration of collective rights in the homeland. The event links everyday commerce to political identity and autonomy. It should be read as an assertion made by an existing people, rather than a claim that a community was created instantly by a battlefield victory.
scenes.note: The map follows this date across every region; zoom out to see other histories.

scenes.title: Negotiating at established gathering places
scenes.body: Treaty 1 at Lower Fort Garry and Treaty 7 at Blackfoot Crossing were separated by six years and involved different nations. Both meetings drew on places already embedded in Indigenous and commercial geography. Crowfoot selected Blackfoot Crossing for a major gathering in 1877; Lower Fort Garry had hosted Anishinaabe and Swampy Cree negotiations in 1871. The points show meetings and participants, not a single advancing frontier line. Their agreements require attention to promises and Indigenous understandings as well as to the documents produced by the Crown.
scenes.note: The map follows this date across every region; zoom out to see other histories.

scenes.title: A residential school in the Qu’Appelle valley
scenes.body: NCTR dates the Catholic residential school at Lebret from 1884. This institution adds a different geography to the regional map: the schooling of Indigenous children alongside expanding treaty and settlement systems. The date marks documented operation, not the beginning of every family’s experience or the age of every building. The school continued beyond this atlas’s 1934 limit. Its inclusion connects political change with the institutions that reached into community life, while reserving individual stories and later events for their own evidence and chronology.
scenes.note: The map follows this date across every region; zoom out to see other histories.

scenes.title: A settlement before and after the battle
scenes.body: Batoche was a ferry crossing, trading place and Métis river-lot settlement before it became a battlefield. Xavier Letendre’s 1872 enterprise connected households with a major trail across the South Saskatchewan River. In May 1885, Canadian forces defeated the Métis defenders after four days of fighting. The battle altered lives and political possibilities, but the community continued. Holding the commercial founding and military confrontation together gives residents more than the role of combatants and makes the persistence of Métis life after defeat visible.
scenes.note: The map follows this date across every region; zoom out to see other histories.

stories.title: Northwest Canada: tools, trade and changing authority
stories.subtitle: Ancient hunting technology, northern exchange, Klondike displacement and treaty encounters.
stories.description: Ancient hunting technology, northern exchange, Klondike displacement and treaty encounters.

scenes.title: A bone and a disputed interpretation
scenes.body: Bluefish Cave II preserves a horse mandible dated to the last glacial maximum. Researchers have argued that marks on it were made during human butchering, while others have questioned site formation and possible natural processes. Both interpretations remain part of the debate over this particular bone. Its significance is a dated observation whose interpretation matters for early human presence, rather than a fully reconstructed settlement. The broader northern story can begin with this uncertainty and still proceed to later, materially different evidence of skilled hunting and community life.
scenes.note: The interpretation of the bone marks remains disputed.

scenes.title: A carefully assembled hunting tool
scenes.body: The southern Yukon dart is much more than a stone point. Its surviving materials include wood, sinew and feathers, while chemical analysis identified beaver castoreum. The published calibrated date places the artifact in the fifth millennium BCE. Preservation in ice makes parts of hunting technology visible that ordinarily decay, allowing a closer view of how different materials worked together. Its presence does not establish the size of a hunting party or a permanent settlement, and this map keeps the exact ice patch undisclosed.
scenes.note: A broad southern-Yukon reference; not an archaeological destination.

scenes.title: A post within Gwich’in and Inuvialuit networks
scenes.body: The Hudson’s Bay Company opened a post near today’s Fort McPherson in 1840, seeking trade with Gwich’in and Inuvialuit. Eight years later the post moved downriver to the later community’s site. This sequence shows why an establishment date and a modern map location are different kinds of information. The Peel River and its surrounding country already supported travel and exchange. Teetł’it zheh’s history therefore includes the company’s commercial initiative within the continuing homeland of the Teetł’it Gwich’in and their wider northern relationships.
scenes.note: The map follows this date across every region; zoom out to see other histories.

scenes.title: Chilkat traders challenge the company
scenes.body: Fort Selkirk stood where the Pelly meets the Yukon, in a landscape of Northern Tutchone fishing and exchange. The Hudson’s Bay Company’s 1848 post intruded into trading relationships linking the interior with the coast. In 1852, Chilkat Tlingit traders attacked the post and expelled the company’s people. The confrontation reveals Indigenous actors defending commercial interests and connections, rather than only reacting to distant imperial decisions. The post’s closure ended one institutional presence, while travel, fishing and Indigenous trading continued through the same river country.
scenes.note: The map follows this date across every region; zoom out to see other histories.

scenes.title: From negotiated trade to displacement
scenes.body: Gàh Ts’yàt’s initiative helped bring the Alaska Commercial Company to Fort Reliance in 1874. Two decades later, the gold rush transformed the scale of newcomers’ presence. Tr’ondëk Hwëch’in were displaced from Tr’ochëk and moved to Moosehide in spring 1897 after negotiations. These events should be read together without treating their outcomes as inevitable. A sought-after trading partnership and a later displacement reveal changing power, while continued travel to fishing and hunting places shows lives extending far beyond the buildings of the new village.
scenes.note: The map follows this date across every region; zoom out to see other histories.

scenes.title: Schools and new community centres
scenes.body: In 1911, Chooutla began the period of operation recorded by Carcross/Tagish First Nation’s residential-school history. The next year, a Hudson’s Bay Company post opened at Aktlarvik / Aklavik, established by the Greenland and Pokiak families. These places involved different communities and institutions, but together they show the varied changes occurring across the north. School administration and Indigenous settlement-building belong in the same regional history without becoming interchangeable experiences. Neither a school’s opening nor a company post’s establishment marks the beginning of people’s relationship to the land.
scenes.note: The map follows this date across every region; zoom out to see other histories.

scenes.title: Questions at the treaty table
scenes.body: At Fort Providence in June 1921, Treaty 11 negotiations addressed more than a signature on a document. The commissioner recorded concerns about access to hunting, fishing and trapping, freedom to travel, medical provision and support. Those questions reveal what was at stake for people whose livelihoods crossed a broad landscape. His report is one side of the documentary record, not a complete account of Dene consent. The signing opened a continuing political relationship whose promises and understandings require more than a point on the map.
scenes.note: The map follows this date across every region; zoom out to see other histories.

stories.title: Arctic Canada: houses, hunting and encounters with the state
stories.subtitle: Explore Arctic occupations, Inuit dwellings, fishing and whaling work through the 1894 chapter.
stories.description: Explore Arctic occupations, Inuit dwellings, fishing and whaling work through the 1894 chapter.

scenes.title: Occupation beside a High Arctic lake
scenes.body: Lake Hazen’s basin provides a setting for a local archaeological observation rather than a single continuous High Arctic settlement story. Rivendell’s occupation is placed around 1000 BCE and discussed in relation to Independence I and Independence II assemblages. Such classifications help researchers compare tools and features through time. They do not identify every individual’s ancestry or explain every change in population. Later Inuit and Inughuit use of the basin belongs to its own history of hunting and fishing in this distinctive northern landscape.
scenes.note: Regional lake reference, not the archaeological site location.

scenes.title: Chronologies that do not change everywhere at once
scenes.body: At Iqaluktuuq on Victoria Island, the existing evidence places Late Dorset activity after 1300 CE. Farther east, Somerset Island preserves Thule Inuit houses and a whaling landscape. Read together, these records show why broad labels need local dates. Material traditions and settlement practices did not change on one universal Arctic timetable. The evidence can support questions about contemporaneity and possible contact while leaving the character of particular encounters unresolved. It cannot turn a shift in artifacts into a claim of extermination or a precise ethnic boundary.
scenes.note: The map follows this date across every region; zoom out to see other histories.

scenes.title: Building warmth near hunting grounds
scenes.body: Qaummaarviit’s surviving evidence includes house remains, tent rings, caches and equipment for work on land and water. Whale bones supported qarmait covered with skins, while lamps provided heat and light. The nearby ice and mainland offered access to seals and caribou. The scene invites attention to the practical construction of shelter and the organisation of a camp. Restored houses help explain those techniques, but they should not be mistaken for untouched medieval buildings or proof that all known structures were occupied at once.
scenes.note: 1500 is a viewing year in a broad activity window.

scenes.title: Fishing grounds and remembered violence
scenes.body: The rapids at Kugluk were a fishing place when Samuel Hearne reached the lower Coppermine region in 1771. His Dene companions attacked Inuit camped there, an encounter remembered in the English name Bloody Falls. Nunavut’s community planning restores Kugluk to the foreground and places the event within a longer history. That approach preserves the violent episode without allowing it to become the only meaning of the landscape. Fishing, movement and continuing Inuit relationships remain part of the same place and deserve equal historical attention.
scenes.note: The map follows this date across every region; zoom out to see other histories.

scenes.title: Whaling work and a sealskin church
scenes.body: Qikiqtan’s shore buildings date from 1857, when commercial whaling drew heavily on Inuit knowledge and labour. Across Cumberland Sound, an Anglican mission opened at Uumanarjuaq in 1894, including a church made from sealskin. The two places show different institutions using the sound’s maritime connections. Work with whalers, new goods and religious teaching created choices and pressures within existing Inuit lives. Their arrival dates do not mark the beginning of local history, and a mission’s foundation cannot stand for everyone’s conversion or abandonment of earlier practices.
scenes.note: The map follows this date across every region; zoom out to see other histories.

scenes.title: A permanent post follows seasonal exchange
scenes.body: At Arviat, seasonal exchange preceded the establishment of a permanent Hudson’s Bay Company post in 1921. The community’s history describes Paallirmiut traders connecting inland and coastal activities and moving goods through wider networks. A store changed opportunities for commerce without instantly gathering every family into permanent town life. This distinction matters on a map where one fixed point can easily conceal seasonal travel. The record marks an institution at a named place while leaving the larger human geography of camps, hunting and exchange visible in the narrative.
scenes.note: The map follows this date across every region; zoom out to see other histories.

scenes.title: Courts and police in an inhabited Arctic
scenes.body: At Pond Inlet in 1923, a Canadian magistrate tried three Inuit for a trader’s death; Nuqallaq was sentenced to imprisonment in Manitoba. Qikiqtani’s history places the trial within threats by the trader and Canada’s effort to assert its law. The next year an RCMP detachment opened at Dundas Harbour. These events reveal the expanding reach of courts and police across established Inuit homelands. They are specific institutional milestones, not evidence that Canadian administration suddenly became complete everywhere or that Inuit law and community decision-making ceased.
scenes.note: The map follows this date across every region; zoom out to see other histories.

stories.title: Aleutian Islands: homes and work across the sea
stories.subtitle: From early blades and stone houses to forced fur labour, village changes and church building
stories.description: The Aleutian and Pribilof islands hold histories of skilled maritime life, enduring villages and profound colonial disruption. Tools, houses, gardens and churches reveal how Unangan communities lived and changed across the centuries through 1895.

scenes.title: The work inside a stone blade
scenes.body: At Anangula, stone cores and the flakes struck from them preserve the work of early toolmakers. Long blades were shaped into implements for cutting and scraping, using raw materials brought from elsewhere. These finds reveal skilled decisions about stone in an early coastal setting. They belong to the ancient blade site, which is separate from the younger village remains elsewhere on the island. A shared island name should not collapse those different histories.
scenes.note: Rounded early-use date from the institutional synthesis, not the foundation year of the later village.

scenes.title: A hearth and another episode later
scenes.body: Charred stones, charcoal, blades and microblades at Amaknak’s Quarry Site place people in a period once poorly represented in the eastern islands. A dated charcoal sample belongs to a possible hearth. Another sample higher in the cultural sequence records a later episode centuries afterward. The two observations expand the known history of activity here, while leaving the interval between them open. They should appear as separate dated evidence, not a single uninterrupted village.
scenes.note: Scene year lies inside 7730–7580 cal BP as encoded by the supplied record; the later sample remains a separate record.

scenes.title: Houses beside a lake on Sanak
scenes.body: At Sandy Dunes, people built small round or oval houses beside a former pond, with hearths along one side. Shell middens preserved remains of fish, birds and mammals. Excavation distinguishes successive areas of habitation, while obsidian attributed to Umnak points to connections beyond this island.
scenes.note: The scene uses the published phase window; the houses represent several episodes of settlement.

scenes.title: Making a home warm and durable
scenes.body: At Amaknak Bridge, partly sunken houses incorporated stone walls, fireplaces, vents and channels beneath their floors. Some had several rooms, and repeated repairs changed the buildings over time. Farther west at Chaluka, generations of houses and daily refuse accumulated beside present-day Nikolski. Together these places show the work of maintaining homes within a maritime economy. They offer a history of household life as well as tools and hunting, without making every structure contemporary.
scenes.note: Representative year within both supplied windows; the Bridge range is a sample envelope, not a lifespan for every house.

scenes.title: Households at the far western islands
scenes.body: Early communities on Agattu and Shemya lived near productive coasts at the western end of the Aleutian chain. Fish, seals and seabirds supplied households, and boats connected neighbouring islands. The regional archaeological synthesis places settlement here by roughly 3,000 years ago. Later changes in fishhooks, cutting tools and other equipment show people adjusting their practices through time. The island references locate that western history without inventing a precise arrival voyage or an excavated-house position.
scenes.note: Rounded source estimate for early local settlement; these are distinct island communities.

scenes.title: Fur hunters bring captivity and violence
scenes.body: In 1745, Russian fur hunters met armed resistance at Agattu and continued to Attu. The historical account records captives taken and an attack in which fifteen Unangan men were killed to seize women. The episode exposes the human cost behind the expansion of maritime commerce. Traders entered inhabited islands with existing communities, households and leadership. This record places violence on Attu without claiming to know the precise location of each confrontation or every participant’s experience.
scenes.note: Named island and year are documented; the marker is not a surveyed attack site.

scenes.title: A sealing workforce moved north
scenes.body: The fur-seal industry drew Unangan men into the Pribilof Islands under coercion. Russian hunting companies forced seasonal journeys from communities farther south, putting maritime skill to work for outside merchants. In 1787, traders established a settlement at or near Marunich on St. Paul. Camps and sod houses became the infrastructure of commercial sealing. This movement differed from ordinary community travel: hunters’ destinations and labour were organized around the demands of an expanding extraction economy.
scenes.note: 1787 lies within the forced-labour attestation window; any connection line is schematic, not a ship’s track.

scenes.title: A settlement with extensive gardens
scenes.body: Around 1820, Russians and Unangan reoccupied Korovinski, long after the ancestral village’s earlier end. Houses, warehouses and a church formed a settlement linked to Russian-American Company administration. Garden plots enclosed by sod walls added cultivated food to the maritime economy, and surviving furrows make that work visible. The return to the same locality did not join the two occupations into one continuous phase. It created another community setting, with new buildings, crops and commercial obligations.
scenes.note: Approximate reoccupation milestone; the ancestral occupation and volcanic disruption are separate evidence.

scenes.title: Permanent homes move, hunters return
scenes.body: In 1823, the Russian-American Company moved Sanak’s population and hunting group to Belkofski in response to declining sea-otter grounds. The move changed permanent residence, but hunters continued to visit Sanak. This distinction matters for reading the landscape: leaving a settlement did not mean abandoning all knowledge, routes or work associated with the island. The company’s decision reorganized community life around commercial priorities, while residents’ continued journeys preserved a relationship with the older place.
scenes.note: Sanak and Belkofski are documented endpoints; no exact sailing route is reconstructed.

scenes.title: A new village, an older landscape
scenes.body: Families leaving Korovinski established present-day Atka around 1870, after a period in which the old settlement had housed Russian-American Company activity. The move unfolded over several years. New permanent homes did not erase the old village from memory or travel: Korovinski remained known through community history and visits. This is another kind of settlement change, one that connects living families with archaeological remains instead of treating an old site’s end as the disappearance of its people.
scenes.note: Approximate establishment date, not a single documented moving day for every household.

scenes.title: Generations of craft in one church
scenes.body: The Church of the Holy Ascension built at Unalaska in 1894–1896 incorporated timbers from earlier churches of 1826 and 1858. Its central spaces, side chapels and bell tower make the building’s cruciform arrangement visible. Inside, Unangan craftsmanship helped shape the church’s religious setting. The construction history therefore belongs to local labour as well as missionary institutions. Reused wood connects different building phases, while each generation’s work changed the form that worshippers encountered.
scenes.note: 1895 is within the documented construction interval; it is not the beginning of the parish or Unangan community.

scenes.title: Winter homes and summer fishing places
scenes.body: In 1909, Jochelson’s expedition reached Chichagof Harbor and then travelled with the Unangan community to Sarana Bay for the summer. This observation catches seasonal movement in progress. A permanent winter village could coexist with fishing camps, gathering places and other seasonal destinations. Leaving houses for part of the year was not the same as abandoning the settlement. The record restores movement to a map that might otherwise make coastal communities look like fixed points.
scenes.note: One documented season, with coastal reference points rather than a reconstructed boat track.

scenes.title: Whaling becomes a shore industry
scenes.body: Akutan’s whaling station opened in 1912, bringing shore-based industrial processing to a harbour already shaped by trade and fishing. Commercial catches included humpback and right whales. The station connected local waters with a larger industry, differing in scale and organization from household subsistence practices. It remained active when this atlas’s chronology ends in 1934. The endpoint closes the map’s selected period, not the station’s operations or the continuing history of the people living around the harbour.
scenes.note: The supplied activity record extends through 1934; the historical station continued to 1939.

scenes.title: Salt cod leaves Pauloff Harbor
scenes.body: At Pauloff Harbor, shore buildings supported a commercial cod fishery. Workers lived in bunkhouses, sorted and salted the catch, and stored it for shipment. In May 1912 John Cobb photographed men loading the schooner Sequoia. The working village was part of a network of fishing shores around Sanak.
scenes.note: A dated photograph anchors this scene; it is not a construction date for every building.

stories.title: Canada: many histories, one shared map
stories.subtitle: Eight regions, connected histories
stories.description: Move between eight regional histories of homes, food, trade, diplomacy, conflict and colonial change, from the earliest evidence to the 1885 chapter.

scenes.title: A bone and a disputed interpretation
scenes.body: Bluefish Cave II preserves a horse mandible dated to the last glacial maximum. Researchers have argued that marks on it were made during human butchering, while others have questioned site formation and possible natural processes. The existing record keeps those arguments visible together. Its significance is a dated observation whose interpretation matters for early human presence, rather than a fully reconstructed settlement. The broader northern story can begin with this uncertainty and still proceed to later, materially different evidence of skilled hunting and community life.
scenes.note: Reuses the existing record and its explicit cut-mark dispute. Other regions remain on the same map date; zoom out to follow their evidence.

scenes.title: Horses and camels at a river crossing
scenes.body: At Wally’s Beach, hunters processed horses and a camel beside an ancient crossing. Cut marks, broken bones and artifacts allow researchers to reconstruct practical work with large animals. Revised radiocarbon analysis places that activity around 13,300 calibrated years before 1950. This scene is about the evidence left by butchering, rather than a complete reconstruction of the hunt. The animals’ later extinction raises larger questions that one locality cannot answer by itself, and several nearby carcasses need not all represent the same day.
scenes.note: Rounded calibrated-age anchor. Other regions remain on the same map date; zoom out to follow their evidence.

scenes.title: Footsteps on a changing shore
scenes.body: A child-sized footprint and larger impressions turn an early coastline into a place where people can be imagined moving, pausing and stepping across wet ground. The Calvert Island assemblage contains 29 identifiable tracks, with associated pine wood dating the surface. It is a brief physical trace within a much larger human history. Changing shorelines help explain why early coastal evidence can be buried or difficult to find, while the tracks themselves do not supply a complete route or settlement history.
scenes.note: Viewing year lies inside the conservative dated envelope; island reference only. Other regions remain on the same map date; zoom out to follow their evidence.

scenes.title: Stone tools after the ice
scenes.body: Debert’s stone tools belong to an early history of people using Atlantic landscapes after the ice retreated. A calibrated synthesis puts its pooled age around 12,630 years before 1950. The site is often pictured as a caribou-hunting place, but its excavations did not recover animal bones. The tools provide direct evidence; the hunted species requires interpretation. This distinction leaves the human story intact while keeping it honest: people worked here, shaped stone and knew a landscape very different from Nova Scotia today.
scenes.note: Approximate viewing year within the existing calibrated range, not a newly calculated first arrival. Other regions remain on the same map date; zoom out to follow their evidence.

scenes.title: A fire at the edge of a caribou crossing
scenes.body: At Kamestastin Lake in the Labrador interior, Tshikapisk excavations found worked quartz in a pit beside a small fire. Charcoal from two contexts dates this work to the sixth millennium BCE. The lake outlet was one of the places where caribou crossed. This evidence opens a view into the lives of people who worked and hunted far from the coast.
scenes.note: The display year lies in the larger published probability component for the dated samples.

scenes.title: Building with water and fish
scenes.body: Wooden stakes at Mnjikaning preserve the work of fish-fence builders at the Narrows between Lakes Simcoe and Couchiching. The earliest dated evidence is placed around 3300 BCE. Concentrated seasonal fish runs made the channel a place where practical skill and collective responsibility mattered. Later Wendat use and Anishinaabeg stewardship belong to its history as well. The marker points to the surrounding public locality, while the surviving underwater structures retain their own protected locations and significance.
scenes.note: Approximate early-use anchor; not a continuous 5,000-year occupation interval. Other regions remain on the same map date; zoom out to follow their evidence.

scenes.title: Building a more productive beach
scenes.body: At northern Quadra Island, low stone walls changed how sediment accumulated along the shore. The resulting terraces enlarged suitable clam habitat and required knowledgeable work with local tides and beach conditions. The dated gardens reveal deliberate food production in Laich-Kwil-Tach and northern Coast Salish homelands. Their history stretches through many construction and maintenance episodes. Reading a wall alongside the shells beneath it and former sea levels is how researchers distinguish an old beach from a garden made and tended by people.
scenes.note: Rounded conservative minimum-age anchor, not the first wall’s exact year. Other regions remain on the same map date; zoom out to follow their evidence.

scenes.title: Occupation beside a High Arctic lake
scenes.body: Lake Hazen’s basin provides a setting for a local archaeological observation rather than a single continuous High Arctic settlement story. Rivendell’s occupation is placed around 1000 BCE and discussed in relation to Independence I and Independence II assemblages. Such classifications help researchers compare tools and features through time. They do not identify every individual’s ancestry or explain every change in population. Later Inuit and Inughuit use of the basin belongs to its own history of hunting and fishing in this distinctive northern landscape.
scenes.note: Regional lake reference, not the archaeological site location. Other regions remain on the same map date; zoom out to follow their evidence.

scenes.title: Sturgeon, wild rice and riverside gathering
scenes.body: At the Rainy River’s Long Rapids, people gathered for sturgeon. Dwellings and Laurel mounds at Kay-Nah-Chi-Wah-Nung preserve part of the history of that place. At Wanipigow Lake, pottery and food remains show the use of wild rice and other plant foods in the forest interior. These are two ways rivers and lakes sustained households and brought them together.
scenes.note: 950 falls in broad pottery phase windows for the two localities.

scenes.title: A precise year of woodworking
scenes.body: Three pieces of wood from Norse archaeological contexts at L’Anse aux Meadows preserve an unusually precise date. Researchers identified a radiocarbon event in annual tree rings and counted outward to the cutting edges: the trees were cut in 1021 CE. This anchors a real episode of work at the settlement. It does not tell us when every building was erected, how long every crew remained, or when all contact began. The precision belongs to the documented activity, not to every part of the site’s story.
scenes.note: Reuse the existing precise-date record; do not duplicate the alternative Norse visit pin. Other regions remain on the same map date; zoom out to follow their evidence.

scenes.title: A larger longhouse village
scenes.body: Droulers/Tsiionhiakwatha preserves a larger settlement than nearby McDonald. A primary artifact study describes seven excavated longhouses and two middens, with abundant worked bone and animal remains. More houses may have existed, but the excavated number is the secure observation. The study’s circa 1490–1515 phase differs from the visitor centre’s circa 1450 date. The architecture and artifacts remain compelling across that disagreement: many households lived, cooked, made tools and negotiated their relationships within a substantial village.
scenes.note: Uses the newer study’s approximate phase; the older public chronology remains documented. Other regions remain on the same map date; zoom out to follow their evidence.

scenes.title: A village’s date changes the history
scenes.body: At Jean-Baptiste Lainé/Mantle, longhouses enclosed a central plaza and defensive works protected the settlement. A new radiocarbon model places the site later than its former circa 1500–1550 dating. This changes how we understand the timing of community aggregation near Lake Ontario. The village contained few European goods, but that absence did not mean it was early or isolated. Different communities participated in different networks, and the histories of their exchange relationships cannot be read from a single imported object.
scenes.note: 1596–1618 is a 68.2% modeled date estimate, not an occupation-duration estimate. Other regions remain on the same map date; zoom out to follow their evidence.

scenes.title: Community rebuilding and regional diplomacy
scenes.body: Wendake’s establishment in 1697 belongs to the history of Huron-Wendat survival and new community life after upheaval in the Great Lakes. Four years later, Wendat diplomacy helped shape the Great Peace of Montréal. Kondiaronk and other Indigenous leaders did political work across long distances, alongside French authorities and delegates from many nations. These events show the river as a connection between living communities. They also show that an agreement grew from negotiation among participants whose interests and experiences were not identical.
scenes.note: The city marker represents the agreement, not a reconstructed conference footprint. Other regions remain on the same map date; zoom out to follow their evidence.

scenes.title: Conquest becomes forced departure
scenes.body: The capture of Fort Beauséjour in 1755 and the confinement of Acadians at Grand-Pré connected military power with civilian removal. Three years later, after Louisbourg fell, British authorities organized deportation from Skmaqn/Port-la-Joye on Île Saint-Jean. Families left an island that had also been a place of Mi’kmaq–French alliance. More than 3,000 French and Acadian inhabitants were removed, and shipwrecks and illness killed many at sea. The departures changed communities across the Atlantic while Mi’kmaq life on Epekwitk continued under new pressures.
scenes.note: These are related events in 1755 and 1758, not a single voyage or one deportation day. Other regions remain on the same map date; zoom out to follow their evidence.

scenes.title: Pemmican and political rights
scenes.body: The encounter at Frog Plain took place within a trade economy sustained by Indigenous food, transport and labour. Cuthbert Grant’s Métis party was moving provisions when it confronted Governor Semple’s party in June 1816. Métis accounts remember the resulting victory as a declaration of collective rights in the homeland. The event links everyday commerce to political identity and autonomy. It should be read as an assertion made by an existing people, rather than a claim that a community was created instantly by a battlefield victory.
scenes.note: Other regions remain on the same map date; zoom out to follow their evidence.

scenes.title: Chilkat traders challenge the company
scenes.body: Fort Selkirk stood where the Pelly meets the Yukon, in a landscape of Northern Tutchone fishing and exchange. The Hudson’s Bay Company’s 1848 post intruded into trading relationships linking the interior with the coast. In 1852, Chilkat Tlingit traders attacked the post and expelled the company’s people. The confrontation reveals Indigenous actors defending commercial interests and connections, rather than only reacting to distant imperial decisions. The post’s closure ended one institutional presence, while travel, fishing and Indigenous trading continued through the same river country.
scenes.note: Other regions remain on the same map date; zoom out to follow their evidence.

scenes.title: A settlement before and after the battle
scenes.body: Batoche was a ferry crossing, trading place and Métis river-lot settlement before it became a battlefield. Xavier Letendre’s 1872 enterprise connected households with a major trail across the South Saskatchewan River. In May 1885, Canadian forces defeated the Métis defenders after four days of fighting. The battle altered lives and political possibilities, but the community continued. Holding the commercial founding and military confrontation together gives residents more than the role of combatants and makes the persistence of Métis life after defeat visible.
scenes.note: Other regions remain on the same map date; zoom out to follow their evidence.

scenes.title: Courts and police in an inhabited Arctic
scenes.body: At Pond Inlet in 1923, a Canadian magistrate tried three Inuit for a trader’s death; Nuqallaq was sentenced to imprisonment in Manitoba. Qikiqtani’s history places the trial within threats by the trader and Canada’s effort to assert its law. The next year an RCMP detachment opened at Dundas Harbour. These events reveal the expanding reach of courts and police across established Inuit homelands. They are specific institutional milestones, not evidence that Canadian administration suddenly became complete everywhere or that Inuit law and community decision-making ceased.
scenes.note: Other regions remain on the same map date; zoom out to follow their evidence.

scenes.title: Children taken into an assimilation system
scenes.body: Shubenacadie residential school opened to students in 1930, after construction in 1928–1929. Many Mi’kmaw and Wolastoqkew children were compelled to attend the federally funded, church-run institution. Its purpose reached beyond instruction: it was part of a system seeking to suppress Indigenous cultures and identities. The official history was developed with representatives acting for Survivors and descendants. The atlas ends in 1934, but the school remained open much longer, and the histories of affected families and communities cannot be confined to that map endpoint.
scenes.note: Opening-to-students event; never display 1934 as the school’s closing date. Other regions remain on the same map date; zoom out to follow their evidence.

scenes.title: Families move as Lac Seul rises
scenes.body: Water impounded by the Ear Falls dam flooded reserve land at Lac Seul without the First Nation’s consent. Families lost homes, gardens, wild rice beds and graves. At Kejick Bay the water turned a connected shore into an island. By the atlas endpoint the Nation was living through the consequences of decisions made elsewhere.
scenes.note: 1934 is the atlas endpoint during the documented rise in water levels.
